considered.reasoning: The archive's best short-side alpha came from exactly this economics (−0.051, t −3.68) but with an unreliable slope (fmb −1.79) because its acquisitiveness leg was a raw asset-scaled dollar intensity; substituting the bounded purchased-share measure that produced the archive's strongest slope is a targeted fix for the metric that was broken. Both legs load positively on the failed acquirer, so the same-signed rank sum keeps the short leg cleanly composed and avoids the multiplicative signing that failed earlier.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: shift_from_buying_to_building
considered.expression: SUMRANK(MA(RATIO(oancf, at), 3), SUB(LAG(RATIO(TS_SUM(COALESCE(aqc, SUB(at, at)), 3), ADD(TS_SUM(COALESCE(aqc, SUB(at, at)), 3), TS_SUM(COALESCE(xrd, SUB(at, at)), 3))), 3), RATIO(TS_SUM(COALESCE(aqc, SUB(at, at)), 3), ADD(TS_SUM(COALESCE(aqc, SUB(at, at)), 3), TS_SUM(COALESCE(xrd, SUB(at, at)), 3)))))
considered.hypothesis: Investors classify firms by their historical identity, so a cash generator that has re-tilted its growth budget away from acquisitions and toward internal development is still priced as the acquirer it used to be, while a firm drifting the other way is not yet penalized for abandoning organic development.
considered.reasoning: The earlier transition test failed (0.013/t 1.20) because it differenced raw asset-scaled acquisition intensity, which moves with deal size and firm growth rather than with allocation policy; differencing the bounded purchased *share* between two non-overlapping three-year windows measures a genuine change in policy mix that is invariant to scale. This is the one mechanism in the winning channel that remains untested in its effective form, and a positive result would show the anomaly responds to changes in allocation behaviour rather than only to its level.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: purchased_share_of_growth_investment
considered.expression: SUB(RANK(MA(RATIO(oancf, at), 3)), RANK(RATIO(TS_SUM(COALESCE(aqc, SUB(at, at)), 5), ADD(TS_SUM(COALESCE(aqc, SUB(at, at)), 5), ADD(TS_SUM(COALESCE(xrd, SUB(at, at)), 5), MAX(SUB(TS_SUM(capx, 5), TS_SUM(dp, 5)), SUB(at, at)))))))
considered.hypothesis: Only spending above the replacement of worn assets represents a growth decision, so the purchased share should be measured against acquisitions plus research plus *net* capacity additions: cash generators whose growth investment is mostly bought are over-credited, while those who grew by developing and expanding organically are neglected.
considered.reasoning:
Including gross capital expenditure would have made the share mechanically decreasing in capital intensity and tilted the long leg toward heavy spenders, contradicting the discipline direction the archive establishes; netting cumulative depreciation out of the capex term removes maintenance spending entirely, so a utility replacing plant is no longer classified as a builder. This preserves the bounded-share construction that produced the archive's strongest slope while widening the denominator only with genuine growth outlays, which also recovers most of the coverage lost when the two-channel share leaves non-spenders undefined.
REASONING_END
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: debt_financed_acquisition_exposure
considered.expression: SUB(RANK(MA(RATIO(oancf, at), 3)), RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(MIN(TS_SUM(COALESCE(aqc, SUB(at, at)), 3), TS_SUM(MAX(DELTA(dltt, 1), SUB(at, at)), 3)), at), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: Purchased growth is most likely to disappoint when the buyer had to borrow for it: heavy acquisition spending overlapping with heavy new long-term borrowing marks a firm that bought assets it could not fund internally and now carries fixed claims against uncertain synergies, whereas a persistent cash generator doing neither is an underpriced cash cow.
considered.reasoning:
The equity-financed analogue of this construction is independently supported in the archive (0.030/t 2.79), and the debt channel is the untested half of the payment-method question — it identifies a different population, since borrowers are typically cash-flow-positive incumbents rather than high-valuation issuers. Using MIN of cumulative deal spending and cumulative new borrowing requires both conditions, so the short leg is specifically leveraged acquirers rather than an additive stack of the separately documented acquisition and debt-issuance effects.
REASONING_END
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: purchased_intangibles_per_dollar_of_revenue
considered.expression: SUB(RANK(MA(RATIO(oancf, at), 3)), RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(COALESCE(intan, SUB(at, at)), sale), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: An acquisition premium is justified only by the business volume it brings: a firm carrying purchased intangibles worth many times its annual revenue has paid for scale it never obtained and faces impairment, whereas a cash generator with little purchased intangible capital relative to its revenue base earned its position operationally.
considered.reasoning:
Prior stock-side tests deflated intangibles by total assets, which makes the leg a balance-sheet mix statement dominated by sector membership; deflating by revenue instead asks whether the price paid is supported by the business acquired, which is the economically meaningful validation test and a scaling never applied to intangibles in this archive. It is therefore not a reparameterization of the tangibility contrast — a capital-light firm and a capital-heavy firm with the same intangibles-to-sales ratio are treated identically here but very differently by asset-share measures.
REASONING_END

critic_notes.rationale: The gating logic is coherent and correctly signed, but it is close to a rediscovery of the well-documented asset-growth anomaly conditioned on profitability (the FF5/q-factor investment-profitability interaction), and the indicator sets roughly half the cross-section to exactly zero, so quintile breakpoints will collapse onto a degenerate zero mass and make portfolio composition unstable.

This is simply free cash flow to assets, a long-published measure (cash-based operating profitability / FCF anomaly) with no genuine cross-theme structure beyond one subtraction, so it is both a rediscovery and too trivial to be worth a test slot.

The denominator (capx + aqc) approaches zero for asset-light and non-investing firms, so the ratio explodes and its sign flips arbitrarily with negative OCF, making the cross-sectional ordering non-monotonic in the hypothesized economics and only cosmetically repaired by 1% winsorization.

A genuinely cross-theme construction whose expression matches the stated hypothesis and sign, with sensible rank-then-difference scaling; the main risks are noisy five-year trends in capx/ppent and coverage loss from the long estimation window.

Despite the "joint profile" claim, nested SUMRANK is a purely additive (and unequally weighted) blend of three separately documented effects — profitability, cash holdings, and capacity-growth — so it tests a generic quality composite rather than any conditional cross-theme mechanism.

Because both factors are bounded ranks, the product's low end is dominated by unprofitable firms rather than by non-expanding profitable firms, so the long leg loads on the wrong side of the profitability anomaly and works directly against the expected negative sign.

This is a single-knob smoothing variant of the already-tested archive winner rather than a new mechanism, and it quietly drops the `aqc` acquisition term from the investment denominator, so a change in performance will be confounded between smoothing and the narrower definition of "investment requirement."

Reduced to its economics this is rank(profitability) minus rank(asset growth) — a near-mechanical composite of the RMW and CMA legs already inside the FF5 benchmark plus the published asset-growth anomaly — so the diagnostic about operator structure is likely to be answered by factor absorption rather than by mispricing, and it re-tests the same channels as the archive signal.

Deflating both the earnings leg and the spending leg by the same installed-capital base is a genuinely coherent construction that measures harvesting versus capacity addition on a common scale, and industry ranking sensibly neutralizes the dominant capital-intensity confound; the main residual risk is partial overlap with the archive's margin-versus-capex divergence signal, which used the same two ratios in trend rather than level form.

The labor-margin channel is genuinely absent from the archive and the expression matches the stated hypothesis, though the reviewer should note that the hiring-rate leg is itself a published anomaly and that `emp` sparsity plus small/zero denominators may compress coverage and destabilize the productivity leg.

The second leg is essentially net external financing (debt issuance plus equity issuance scaled by assets), making the signal a direct rediscovery of the well-documented external-financing/net-issuance anomaly combined with a cash-flow profitability sort, with little incremental content beyond published results and the FF5 legs.

Recasting the winning coverage ratio as an own-history position poses a substantively different level-versus-transition hypothesis rather than a cosmetic tweak, but a 5-observation annual TS_RANK is a very coarse, discretized variable that will blunt cross-sectional dispersion and may mechanically weaken the Fama-MacBeth slope for reasons unrelated to the economics.

This is a pure horizon/smoothing knob on the archive's `cash_coverage_of_required_investment` (identical numerator, denominator, floor, and winsorization, only summed over three years), exactly the kind of cosmetic variant the objective warns against, and it will be highly correlated with the original rather than a distinguishable test.

The construction is structurally identical to the archive's `margin_up_capex_down_divergence` (rank of 5-year profitability trend minus rank of 5-year capex-intensity trend) with only input substitutions (oancf for oibdp, at for ppent), so it is an input swap on an already-evaluated design rather than a new mechanism, and the two trend series will be strongly correlated.

The within-firm capex-versus-own-norm leg is a genuinely new, continuous construct that is not spanned by cross-sectional CMA/asset-growth, the diagnosis of why the earlier TS_RANK version failed is credible, and the profitability leg is measured consistently with the archive's better performers — though the reviewer should verify MA(capx,5) does not include the contemporaneous capx in a way that mechanically compresses dispersion.

The working-capital investment channel is economically distinct from everything in the archive and reacts on a shorter cycle, but the inventory-growth-minus-sales-growth leg is itself a well-documented fundamental-analysis signal (Lev–Thiagarajan, Abarbanell–Bushee, Thomas–Zhang), so the incremental content rests entirely on the interaction with persistent cash profitability.

GROWTH(oiadp) is ill-defined when base-year operating income is negative or near zero, which makes the cross-sectional rank of the first leg partly noise-driven for a nontrivial share of firms, and the resulting construct is close to a coarse change-in-return-on-capital measure already spanned by profitability-growth/expected-growth factors.

The hypothesis is internally inconsistent — it argues R&D is a discretionary *investment*, which implies it belongs in the denominator (investment requirement), yet the expression adds it only to the numerator — so the signal mechanically becomes coverage plus R&D-intensity-scaled-by-capex and will load on the known R&D-intensity anomaly rather than testing the stated mismeasurement channel.

This is a pure preprocessing wrapper (IND_ZSCORE) around the archive's existing best signal with no new economic content, i.e., exactly the kind of cosmetic single-knob variant the objective says to avoid, and the "is it a sector bet" question could be answered by a sector-attribution diagnostic rather than a new signal slot.

The MIN conjunction is a genuinely different functional form for testing whether profitability and asset-growth discipline interact rather than blend, though the two ingredient legs are both well-documented anomalies (Novy-Marx profitability, Cooper-Gulen-Schill asset growth) and it overlaps materially with profit_weighted_operating_asset_discipline, so any gain must come purely from the operator.

The depreciation floor is a well-motivated fix for the small-denominator noise that plausibly killed the 3-year version's FMB slope, but bundling it with a window extension from 3 to 5 years confounds attribution and the change-in-earnings numerator makes this partly a slow-moving profitability-growth signal.

Scaling the internal-funding gap by liquid slack introduces a balance-sheet dimension the archive has not tested and the negative sign matches the expression's natural direction, though it is close in spirit to published external-financing-need/net-financing anomalies and mixes a flow numerator with a partly stock denominator, so a high correlation with cash_coverage_of_required_investment should be checked.

Cumulative five-year acquisition spending is a distinct construct from the one-year goodwill change and the serial-acquirer hypothesis is economically coherent, but serial-acquirer underperformance is itself a published result and the profitability leg is unchanged, so this is an extension rather than a new mechanism.

Replacing the raw hiring rate (a documented stand-alone anomaly) with hiring relative to realized sales growth is a defensible diagnosis-driven fix, but it reuses the exact "growth minus sales growth" template from the inventory-overbuild signal with a different input and inherits the emp-driven coverage and reporting-lag weaknesses that likely hurt the earlier labor test.

This is a mechanical ensemble of the archive's two best-performing signals rather than a new mechanism, and the two legs overlap substantially (both are cash-flow-versus-investment constructs, with the acquisition leg already paired with an oancf-based profitability rank), so the archive's own SUMRANK precedent (self_funding_plus_investment_payoff, alpha diluted to 0.029/t 1.96) predicts averaging-down rather than incremental insight.

Re-deflating cumulative acquisitions by the firm's own cumulative organic investment instead of assets is a substantive composition-versus-scale test with a clear diagnostic payoff either way, though it remains a deflator refinement of an already-successful archive signal and the depreciation-floored denominator will behave erratically for asset-light acquirers.

The COALESCE-to-zero plus MAX(.,dp) construction means the majority of firms with little or no goodwill are scored purely by oancf/dp, so the signal is a mixture of a cash-flow-to-depreciation profitability ratio (which will dominate the long leg) and a goodwill-intensity ratio, making the computed quantity inconsistent with the stated stale-acquisition-premium hypothesis and confounded with the known goodwill-to-assets anomaly.

The diagnosis is legitimate and specific — an after-depreciation earnings numerator is mechanically depressed by the same capex sitting in the denominator — and substituting operating cash flow breaks that link while retaining the depreciation-floored cumulative denominator, making this a mechanism-driven fix rather than a horizon or scaling tweak.

The transition dimension of this exact ratio was already tested and failed in the archive (own_history_position_of_funding_coverage), and a raw first difference of an unbounded, depreciation-floored ratio is scale-dependent and dominated by transitory capex/cash-flow noise, so the discretization diagnosis is plausible but not enough to make this substantively different rather than a re-transformation of a failed construct.

Benchmarking five-year cumulative capex against five-year cumulative depreciation is an economically meaningful replacement-rate standard that is distinct from both the own-mean norm and the cross-sectional asset-growth channel already tested, and the null and positive outcomes carry different, informative interpretations — though the sub-replacement leg will be correlated with the classic investment/CMA factor and the profitability-minus-investment rank-difference form has repeatedly produced weak FF5 alphas in this archive.

This is algebraically almost the same object as the archive's cash_coverage_of_required_investment (oancf/max(capx+aqc, dp), alpha 0.041, t 3.36) — surplus cash deflated by depreciation is a reparametrization of that same coverage ratio using identical inputs — so it is a cosmetic re-scaling rather than a new mechanism, and free-cash-flow-to-capital-consumption is itself close to published FCF/investment-anomaly territory.

The construct is coherent and sign-consistent, but it is essentially spanned by three existing archive signals (cash_generation_vs_acquisitive_expansion, cash_generation_vs_serial_acquisitiveness, unearned_goodwill_without_cash_flow_growth) and amounts to swapping one already-tested leg for another already-tested leg, i.e. a component recombination rather than a new economic channel.

Economically sensible and internally consistent, but it differs from cash_flow_payoff_on_cumulative_investment only by adding aqc to the denominator — a single-term tweak with identical data requirements, so the claim that it will lift coverage above 0.064 is unfounded and the proposal reads as a robustness variant rather than a substantively different design.

Extending the funding-gap numerator to a three-year cumulative deficit while holding the liquidity buffer contemporaneous is a legitimate persistence test (chronic external dependence vs a transitory capex spike) with a correctly signed expression, though the mixed flow/stock deflator MAX(che, TS_SUM(dp,3)) makes the units of the ratio firm-dependent and should be diagnosed if results diverge from the one-year version.

The hypothesis says the cash cow must be "not merely high but steady," yet the expression contains no cash-flow *level* at all — a firm with negligible but placid cash flow scores maximally — and the low-volatility leg largely rediscovers the known earnings/cash-flow-volatility and low-risk anomalies rather than adding a cross-theme interaction.

The "mix" is not actually measured: firms with zero R&D score identically whether they are serial acquirers or pure non-investors, so for the bulk of the cross-section the second leg collapses to R&D/depreciation — i.e. the well-documented R&D-intensity anomaly stacked on a cash-profitability rank — rather than a build-versus-buy contrast.

This is a deflator swap on the archive's leading signal (internal_versus_purchased_growth_spending_mix, alpha 0.064/t 4.74) with an identical profitability leg and an identical R&D-minus-acquisition contrast, i.e. precisely the kind of cosmetic variant the objective warns against, and the program denominator itself contains aqc so the "sourcing tilt" and the deflator move together in a mechanically confounded way.

The stock-versus-flow reframing is a genuinely different horizon and investor error than the archive's spending-window tests and the sign is coherent for *purchased* (balance-sheet) intangibles, but the tangibility-minus-intangibility leg is heavily industry-determined and overlaps the known goodwill-intensity and asset-tangibility characteristics, so it should be industry-neutralized before it can be credited as novel.

This is a mechanical ensemble of two already-evaluated archive signals, and the stated justification is factually wrong — both legs are driven by aqc (it sits in the coverage denominator and is subtracted in the sourcing leg), so the claimed independence that motivates the attribution test does not hold.

Revenue deflation of both legs is a scaling the archive has not used and reframes the mechanism as business-model capital intensity rather than balance-sheet harvesting, the sign convention (NEG on capital formation) matches the hypothesis, and using ΔPP&E-gross plus inventory rather than capex is a defensible refinement — though the cash-margin leg is close to published cash-based operating profitability and the sales deflator will carry strong industry tilts.

This is the third deflator applied to the same profitability-minus-acquisition-intensity construct already tested at asset scale (0.047/t 3.75) and program scale (0.048/t 4.01), and deflating acquisitions by the firm's own cash flow reintroduces oancf on both sides of the difference, making any improvement hard to attribute to the sourcing mechanism.

The hypothesis is explicitly interactive ("acquiring *when* profitability peaks") but SUMRANK is additive, so a high-own-cycle-profitability non-acquirer is scored identically to a trough-cycle acquirer, and since the profitability leg on its own should predict returns positively it works directly against the stated negative sign, leaving the signal essentially a repackaged acquisition-intensity bet.

This is a mechanical ensemble of the archive's two top performers built from the same underlying `xrd`/`aqc` series, so the "partly independent measurement error" claim is doubtful and the outcome will be largely bounded by the two parents — a cosmetic blend rather than a new mechanism.

A strict ablation of an already-evaluated signal and therefore low in novelty, but it is a cheap, decisive attribution test of whether the R&D leg carries any incremental content, and the expression matches the hypothesis; note the coarse 0–5 integer leg and that `COALESCE(aqc,0)` conflates missing with genuinely zero acquisition activity.

R&D-to-assets and capex-to-assets are both long-published anomalies and their difference plus a profitability level is close to a linear recombination of known factors, and the tangible/intangible mix is dominated by sector membership rather than capital-allocation choice, so the "falsification test" framing does not rescue it from being a rediscovery.

A defensible diagnosis-driven repair whose IND_ZSCORE genuinely alters the ordering rather than being monotone-neutral, though it remains one operator away from an already-failed archive signal and leaves the profitability leg un-neutralized, so the asymmetry may limit interpretability of a null result.

The two legs are conceptually and mechanically distinct from prior variants (margin *trend* rather than asset-yield level, paired with acquisition intensity), the sign follows naturally from the expression, and the substitution is motivated by an actual precision result in the archive; watch for instability of TREND on a sales-deflated ratio when sales are small or negative.

Internally consistent — both legs load positively on the "failed acquirer," so the negative expected sign is correct — and the flow-based reformulation with a same-signed rank sum is a reasonable fix for the weak slope of the goodwill version, but it sits close to two existing archive signals (serial acquisitiveness and goodwill-validation) and to the published acquirer-underperformance literature, limiting how much genuinely new information it can deliver.

Industry-neutralizing the R&D-minus-acquisition leg is a substantive (not cosmetic) test of whether the archive's best signal is a firm-level allocation effect or a disguised pharma/software-versus-conglomerate sector tilt, and the precedent from the built-versus-bought stock signal shows the transform is not monotone in its effect.

The subsumption test is legitimately informative, but the claim that the legs are independent is overstated — asset-light R&D-intensive firms mechanically have small capex/dp denominators and therefore inflated payoff ratios, so the two legs are economically correlated even though they share no raw variable.

Sign direction and construction are internally consistent and the peak-deal leg is a genuine measurement change, but it rebuilds an already-tested short-side signal from two archive legs, one of which (the five-year cash-margin trend) had an essentially zero cross-sectional slope on its own, so the hoped-for fmb improvement rests on thin evidence.

A difference of two three-year moving averages is close to a rescaled five-year OLS slope and will be highly correlated with the TREND version, so with an unchanged second leg this is a cosmetic estimator swap on an already-evaluated signal rather than a substantively different construction.

The expression contrasts a five-year cumulative R&D intensity against a single-year peak acquisition intensity, so the scale mismatch means the "contrast" will be dominated by the R&D sum and will mostly reproduce the existing mix signal rather than testing whether large deals are the locus of mispricing.

Because cumulative depreciation exceeds cumulative R&D for the large majority of firms, MAX(xrd5, dp5) collapses to dp5 and the signal becomes acquisitions per dollar of capital consumption — a near-rediscovery of the already-tested acquisitive_share_of_investment_program — so the stated "build-versus-buy tilt" mechanism does not match what the expression computes.

This is essentially the archive's best signal with one term added to the denominator, and the change is not innocuous — putting five-year capex in the denominator makes the "purchased share" mechanically decreasing in capital intensity, so the long leg tilts toward high-capex firms, directly opposing the investment-discipline direction the rest of the archive establishes and confounding the coverage gain with a new sector/capital-intensity exposure.

Despite the disclaimer, this is an averaging of the archive's two top-performing signals whose legs (purchased share of growth budget and count of acquisition years) are near-mechanically correlated, so it will almost certainly land between them and teach nothing about mechanism, with the arbitrary 1:2 nested-SUMRANK weighting adding a free parameter rather than an economic hypothesis.

The self-accumulated-versus-purchased intangible comparison is a genuinely new and well-motivated framing of the accounting-mismeasurement story, though the R&D-to-assets leg risks reducing the result to the well-documented R&D-intensity anomaly and the absence of industry neutralization is a known weakness in this exact channel given the archive's earlier tangibility results.

This is a near-monotone reparameterization of the already-tested industry_neutral_built_versus_bought_stock (difference of intan/at and ppent/at recast as intan/(intan+ppent), same industry z-score, same cash-profit leg), i.e. a cosmetic deflator change to an evaluated signal rather than a new mechanism.

Replacing the raw asset-scaled acquisition intensity with the bounded purchased share is a defensible, specifically diagnosed fix to the weak Fama-MacBeth slope of the earlier failed-acquirer short, but the test should be interpreted cautiously since the three-year cash-flow-change leg is itself a strong standalone predictor and may carry most of the alpha.

Testing a change in the bounded allocation mix across non-overlapping windows is a substantively different (level versus transition) question and is properly motivated by why the raw-intensity version failed, though the share degenerates to a noisy 0/1 flip for non-R&D firms and is undefined for firms doing neither, so coverage and composition stability need checking before any positive result is believed.
